Revendiquer la joie noire est aussi un a: Claiming Black joy is also an act of activism

Le mois de février est depuis plusieurs: For several years now, February has been a month of celebration and reflection on the struggles of Black communities. Journalist Jennifer Da Veiga Rocha wanted to write a story on Black joy, focusing on the collective Black Joy MTL, but she was short on time, so La Converse asked me to take over the subject so the report could be published before the end of Black History Month.
Comme je suis moi-même issue de la commu: As someone who is Black myself, I was drawn to the idea of Black joy existing in public space, just as much as to the idea of writing an article about it. My goal was simple: to shine a light on the collective Black Joy MTL and broaden the conversation about how Black communities can fight their battles differently. I was able to speak with the collective’s co-founders, Claire-Anse Saint-Éloi and Diane Gistal, who shared their vision and told me the story behind their initiative.
J’aurais souhaité recueillir d’autres té: I would have liked to gather more voices – including restaurant owners with established businesses in Montréal, media personalities, artists, and Black people born in Canada and elsewhere – to explore the diversity of experiences tied to Black joy. But, unfortunately, I too ran out of time.
Un vox pop réalisé à la sortie du Collèg: A vox pop conducted outside Collège de Maisonneuve did allow me to include other perspectives. Although the sample remains limited, these conversations raise a broader question: is Black joy an intentional undertaking, or is it simply lived, without being named?
Alors que le Mois de l’histoire des Noir: As Black History Month draws to a close, this report highlights another facet of the Black experience: that of celebration and of creating spaces where people can simply be. I’m happy to present my first article for La Converse.
La 34<sup>e </sup>édition du Mois de l’h: The 34<sup>th </sup>edition of Black History Month is coming to an end. This year’s theme was “All That We Are.” It is a month to celebrate and honour, but also to recall past and present struggles. February marks all of that and, symbolically, the assassination of Malcolm X.
Mais, depuis 1965, comment la résistance: But since 1965, how has the resistance of Black communities been reinvented? Among its forms is one that stands out: Black joy. In Montréal, it is making its mark in public space thanks to the collective Black Joy MTL. It is a movement that doesn’t call for revolt, but resists differently. Because claiming joy is also an act of activism. The collective’s goal? To allow Black people to reclaim their history, to see themselves through the lens of celebration, and no longer only of struggle.
2020 a été un tournant. C’est en plein c: 2020 was a turning point. It was in the midst of the worldwide upheaval sparked by the deaths of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor that Claire-Anse Saint-Éloi and Diane Gistal decided to create Black Joy MTL.
« C’était étouffant. On avait besoin de: “It was suffocating. We needed to breathe, to see something other than pain and anger,” says Diane Gistal. “We were really in a very negative space, exhausted,” adds Claire-Anse Saint-Éloi.
Toutes deux se rappellent avoir ressenti: Both remember feeling a deep fatigue at the ever-present depiction of violence against Black bodies in public spaces and in the media. “You have this anger that consumes you, that has to be transformed. And we told ourselves that resistance can also come through joy,” Diane explains.
Pour les cofondatrices, la joie noire ré: For the co-founders, Black joy lies in life’s simple pleasures: family, community, healing. It all began with a photo project and a picnic at Parc La Fontaine, in Montréal. The idea was simple: bring Black women together for a moment of celebration, with no pretext other than being together.
« Voir une dizaine de femmes noires, tou: “Seeing a dozen Black women, all in yellow and orange, laughing and sharing a moment, was unusual. We felt that joy, but we also saw the effect it had on others,” Claire-Anse remembers. That seemingly trivial moment became a powerful symbol: that of the ability to exist outside of narratives of pain.
« Malheureusement, souvent, quand on se: “Unfortunately, when we gather, it’s often to demand something. Getting together without having to talk about our identity, just to celebrate it, did us a lot of good,” she says.
La joie noire est donc, pour elle, un ac: For her, Black joy is therefore an intentional act. “This intention of coming together, of building community. I think that’s how it shows up, this Black joy,” she continues.
C’est aussi ce que pense Joyce, étudiant: Joyce, a student at Collège de Maisonneuve, thinks so too, even though she was not familiar with the Black joy movement as such. “I’m big on reconciliation,” she says. “The past was awful, but living in the past is like closing yourself off.” For her, although systemic racism exists in Canada, Black joy still has its place.
Beryl, étudiante en ingénierie, partage: Beryl, an engineering student, shares this view, but she, too, had not heard of the Black joy movement. After learning what it was, she says she prioritizes Black joy in her daily life, while pointing out the lack of representation of Black communities in her field of study.
Black Joy MTL a fait le choix de ne pas: Black Joy MTL has chosen not to centre its activities on issues of racism and discrimination. The primary goal is to create spaces where members of Black communities, regardless of age, can come together and celebrate their cultures through a variety of activities.
Une femme et une fillette lors de Porte: A woman and a little girl at Porte tes couleurs avec fierté (Wear your colours with pride), an event organized by the collective Black Joy MTL. Credit: Kiskeya
« Un jour, un jeune est venu me voir et: “One day, a young person came up to me and said: ‘Why are there so many Black kids here? I think it’s great, it doesn’t happen to me often,’” Claire-Anse recounts. Far from isolated, this episode underscores the importance of spaces devoted to Black joy, which nurture a sense of belonging.
Claire-Anse met par ailleurs en avant la: Claire-Anse also highlights the complexity of being a Black person in spaces where you often have to watch yourself. “I have to watch how I speak, my passion, the tone I use. So for me, finding myself in this space, being able to build community, it lets me preserve my strength too and have safe spaces where I can simply be myself, unconditionally. And that’s rare, because everywhere else, I have to be performing, unfortunately.”
Pour la suite, Claire-Anse espère que Bl: Looking ahead, Claire-Anse hopes Black Joy MTL will keep creating these spaces for reflection and celebration, while having a lasting impact on Black communities. “Our identities are changing. Having places to talk about that is essential. I have faith in the future. I hope we can take up even more space and reach more people.”
Le collectif est actuellement à un momen: The collective is currently at a turning point. “We’re asking ourselves: do we become an organization? What are the next projects we’ll take on?” says Diane. Together with Claire-Anse, she wants to give their approach more structure by reflecting on Black Joy MTL’s values, mission and mandate.
Dans ce processus, elles constatent que: In this process, they note that demand for their events remains strong. “People contact us regularly to ask when our next activities will be. You can feel there’s a need,” concludes Claire-Anse. However, the co-founders want to make sure they do things right, by securing partnerships and funding that will guarantee their initiatives remain accessible. “Our last project was able to be free thanks to a major partner who allowed us to cover accessibility costs, like transportation for the kids,” reports Diane.
Elles réfléchissent aussi à la mise en p: They are also thinking about setting up a committee so they aren’t speaking only on their own behalf. “We’re sometimes asked to speak for the entire community, but we really want to create an intergenerational and intercultural dialogue. There are cultures within Black cultures, and we want to be intentional in everything we do,” she concludes.
Black Joy MTL rappelle qu’il existe mill: Black Joy MTL is a reminder that there are a thousand ways to honour the legacy of Black communities. By choosing joy as an act of resistance, the collective is redefining spaces of memory and identity, affirming that celebrating is also a way of passing things on. Through their events, Claire-Anse and Diane are opening a path where being Black can be lived fully, without justification or struggle. It is a way of anchoring Black joy in the collective landscape, well beyond Black History Month.
